label: reference

text: Explaining why physical processes in the brain are accompanied by subjective experience at all is a distinct and harder problem than explaining cognitive functions like attention or reportability.
label: fact

text: Frank Jackson, 'Epiphenomenal Qualia', Philosophical Quarterly 32 (1982) 127-136, presents the Mary thought experiment to argue that complete physical knowledge leaves out facts about phenomenal experience.
label: reference

text: A scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows every physical fact about color vision still learns something new when she sees red for the first time, suggesting that not all facts are physical facts.
label: fact

text: Hilary Putnam, 'The Meaning of Meaning', in Mind, Language and Reality (Cambridge University Press, 1975), uses the Twin Earth thought experiment to argue that meanings are not purely in the head.
label: reference

text: Two speakers in internally identical brain states can nonetheless mean different things by the same word when their physical and social environments differ, so linguistic meaning depends in part on the external world.
label: fact

text: Saul Kripke, Naming and Necessity (Harvard University Press, 1980), defends a causal-historical theory of reference for proper names against the descriptivist view.
label: reference

text: Proper names typically refer to their bearers through a causal-historical chain reaching back to an initial baptism, rather than by expressing some set of descriptions that uniquely identify the bearer.
label: fact

text: W. V. O. Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism', The Philosophical Review 60 (1951) 20-43, attacks the analytic-synthetic distinction and reductionist verificationism.
label: reference

text: There is no principled distinction between purely analytic truths and synthetic empirical truths, and our beliefs face the tribunal of experience only as a holistic web rather than one by one.
label: fact

text: Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (University of Chicago Press, 1962), argues that mature sciences develop through alternating periods of normal science and revolutionary paradigm shifts.
label: reference

text: Scientific progress is not uniformly cumulative but proceeds through long stretches of normal puzzle-solving within a shared framework punctuated by revolutionary changes in fundamental assumptions.
label: fact

text: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (Hutchinson, 1959), argues that the distinctive mark of scientific theories is falsifiability rather than verifiability.
label: reference

text: A theory counts as genuinely scientific only if it makes predictions that could in principle be falsified by observation, since no finite set of confirming instances can establish a universal claim.
label: fact

text: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40), Book III, Part I, Section I, observes the shift from 'is' to 'ought' propositions and questions its justification.
label: reference

text: A normative conclusion about what ought to be the case cannot be validly derived from purely descriptive premises about what is the case without the aid of some further normative premise.
label: fact

text: G. E. Moore, Principia Ethica (Cambridge University Press, 1903), deploys the open-question argument against identifying the good with any natural property.
label: reference

text: For any proposed natural property identified with goodness, it remains a genuinely open question whether things with that property are good, suggesting that goodness is not identical with any such property.
label: fact

text: John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism (Parker, Son and Bourn, 1863), defends the greatest happiness principle as the foundation of morals.
label: reference

text: Actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness, with happiness understood as pleasure and the absence of pain.
label: fact

text: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), proposes a felicific calculus measuring pleasures and pains by intensity, duration, certainty, and related features.
label: reference

text: The moral evaluation of an action depends on the aggregate of pleasures and pains it produces, assessed along dimensions such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent.
label: fact

text: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, identifies the human good with eudaimonia, understood as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life.
label: reference

text: The human good is a life of activity exercising the characteristic excellences of a rational being, sustained throughout a complete life rather than experienced in isolated moments.
label: fact

text: Peter Singer, 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality', Philosophy and Public Affairs 1 (1972) 229-243, argues that affluent people are morally obligated to give substantially to prevent suffering from famine.
label: reference

text: If one can prevent serious suffering at no comparable moral cost, one is morally required to do so, which implies that affluent individuals are obligated to donate a large share of their resources to relieve extreme poverty.
label: fact

text: Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'A Defense of Abortion', Philosophy and Public Affairs 1 (1971) 47-66, uses the violinist thought experiment to argue that even granting fetal personhood, abortion can be morally permissible.
label: reference

text: Even if the fetus is granted the moral status of a person, a pregnant person is not always morally required to sustain that life with her own body, because no one has an unconditional right to use another person's body.
label: fact

text: Philippa Foot, 'The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect', Oxford Review 5 (1967) 5-15, introduces the trolley case and distinguishes doing from allowing harm.
label: reference

text: There is a morally significant distinction between directly killing a smaller number of people as a means and merely diverting a harm so that a smaller number are killed as a side effect.
label: fact

text: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books, 1974), defends a minimal state and an entitlement theory of distributive justice based on just acquisition and transfer.
label: reference

text: A distribution of holdings is just if it arises from an initially just acquisition of unowned resources followed by voluntary transfers, and redistribution beyond what a minimal state requires violates individual rights.
label: fact

text: Ronald Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (Harvard University Press, 1977), argues that individual rights function as trumps over collective goals grounded in background utility.
label: reference

text: Individual moral rights set side constraints that override ordinary appeals to aggregate welfare, so a government may not violate an individual's right merely because doing so would maximize overall social utility.
label: fact

text: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (John W. Parker and Son, 1859), defends the harm principle as the sole legitimate ground for coercive interference with individual liberty.
label: reference

text: The only ground on which society is entitled to restrict an adult's liberty against his will is to prevent harm to others, and neither his own good nor moral disapproval by others suffices.
label: fact

text: H. L. A. Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958) 593-629, defends legal positivism against Lon Fuller's natural law critique.
label: reference

text: The existence and content of a legal system is one question and its moral merit is another, so a rule can be legally valid even when it fails to satisfy moral demands.
label: fact

text: John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980) 417-457, uses the Chinese Room thought experiment to argue that syntactic symbol manipulation is insufficient for semantic understanding.
label: reference

text: A system that produces intelligent-seeming responses purely by manipulating symbols according to formal rules does not thereby understand the language it appears to use, because syntax does not suffice for semantics.
label: fact

text: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind 59 (1950) 433-460, proposes the imitation game as an operational test for machine intelligence.
label: reference

text: A reasonable operational criterion for machine intelligence is whether a machine can hold a text-based conversation indistinguishable from that of a human interlocutor to a blinded judge.
label: fact

text: Daniel Dennett, The Intentional Stance (MIT Press, 1987), argues that ascribing beliefs and desires is a predictive strategy rather than the discovery of intrinsic mental states.
label: reference

text: Treating a system as a rational agent that holds beliefs and desires is a predictive strategy that works whenever doing so yields reliable predictions of behavior, independently of the system's internal composition.
label: fact

text: David Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds (Blackwell, 1986), defends modal realism on which possible worlds are concrete entities as real as our own world.
label: reference

text: A claim that something is possible is to be analyzed as saying that there is some concrete world, spatiotemporally isolated from ours, in which that thing is the case.
label: fact

text: Saul Kripke, Naming and Necessity (Harvard University Press, 1980), argues that identity statements involving rigid designators, such as 'water is H2O', are necessary a posteriori truths.
label: reference

text: Some truths can be known only through empirical investigation and yet are necessary, because an identity between two rigid designators holds in every possible world in which either refers.
label: fact

text: W. V. O. Quine, 'On What There Is', Review of Metaphysics 2 (1948) 21-38, proposes that to be is to be the value of a bound variable in our best regimented theory.
label: reference

text: Our ontological commitments are just those entities that must be taken to exist for our best regimented theories of the world to come out true, identified by what their quantifiers range over.
label: fact

text: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV, poses the problem of the rational justification of inductive inference.
label: reference

text: No non-circular argument shows that the future will resemble the past, since any such argument either presupposes induction or relies on an ungrounded principle of the uniformity of nature.
label: fact

text: Nelson Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast (Harvard University Press, 1955), introduces the predicate 'grue' to pose the new riddle of induction.
label: reference

text: Any body of evidence that confirms 'all emeralds are green' equally confirms a gerrymandered hypothesis such as 'all emeralds are grue', so inductive support depends on which predicates are taken as projectible.
label: fact

text: Bernard Williams, 'Internal and External Reasons', in Moral Luck (Cambridge University Press, 1981), argues that all genuine reasons for action must connect to an agent's existing motivational set.
label: reference

text: A consideration counts as a reason for an agent to act only if a sound deliberative route leads from that agent's existing desires, commitments, and projects to the action in question.
label: fact

text: T. M. Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (Harvard University Press, 1998), defends a contractualist account on which an act is wrong if its performance would be disallowed by any principle no one could reasonably reject.
label: reference

text: An act is morally wrong just when it is forbidden by some principle for the general regulation of behavior that no one, suitably motivated to find terms of cooperation, could reasonably reject.
label: fact

text: Thomas Nagel, The View from Nowhere (Oxford University Press, 1986), explores the tension between subjective and objective standpoints in epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics.
label: reference

text: Human thought occupies both an engaged, subjective standpoint and a detached, impersonal standpoint, and many philosophical problems arise from the difficulty of integrating the two views.
label: fact

text: Plato, Republic, Books II-IV, argues that justice in the soul consists in each part performing its proper function under the rule of reason.
label: reference

text: Justice in the individual consists in a harmonious ordering of rational, spirited, and appetitive parts of the soul, with reason ruling the other two parts.
label: fact

text: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 94, articulates natural law as the rational creature's participation in the eternal law.
label: reference

text: Basic moral principles are grasped by practical reason reflecting on the natural inclinations of rational beings toward goods such as life, sociability, and knowledge.
label: fact

text: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (Andrew Crooke, 1651), Part I Chapter 13, describes life in the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'.
label: reference

text: In the absence of a common power able to enforce peace, human beings would live in a condition of war of all against all in which life would be insecure, impoverished, and brief.
label: fact

text: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (Awnsham Churchill, 1689), Second Treatise Chapter V, grounds private property in the mixing of one's labor with an unowned thing.
label: reference

text: A person acquires a rightful property in a previously unowned natural resource when he mixes his own labor with it, provided that enough and as good is left for others.
label: fact

text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Du Contrat Social (Marc-Michel Rey, 1762), argues that legitimate political authority rests on the general will of the people.
label: reference

text: Legitimate political authority is grounded in a general will that aims at the common good of the political community, as distinct from the aggregated private wills of its members.
label: fact

text: G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), Section IV.A, presents the master-slave dialectic as a stage in the development of self-consciousness through mutual recognition.
label: reference

text: Self-consciousness develops through a struggle for recognition in which the relation between a dominating and a dominated consciousness ultimately proves unstable because genuine self-understanding requires recognition by an equal.
label: fact

text: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality (C. G. Naumann, 1887), traces the historical origins of moral concepts such as good, evil, guilt, and bad conscience.
label: reference

text: Modern moral concepts have a contingent historical origin in particular social practices and psychological dynamics, and tracing that origin can expose their tacit assumptions and power relations.
label: fact

text: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (Blackwell, 1953), sections 243-315, presents the private language argument against the possibility of a purely private sensation language.
label: reference

text: A language whose words refer only to sensations knowable to a single speaker cannot support a genuine distinction between correctly and incorrectly applying a term, and so cannot be a language at all.
label: fact

text: Gottlob Frege, 'Uber Sinn und Bedeutung', Zeitschrift fur Philosophie und philosophische Kritik 100 (1892) 25-50, distinguishes sense (Sinn) from reference (Bedeutung) for linguistic expressions.
label: reference

text: Two expressions can share a referent while differing in the cognitive mode of presentation associated with them, so the meaning of an expression includes more than just the object it picks out.
label: fact

text: Carl Hempel and Paul Oppenheim, 'Studies in the Logic of Explanation', Philosophy of Science 15 (1948) 135-175, articulate the deductive-nomological model of scientific explanation.
label: reference

text: On one influential view, a scientific explanation of an event is a sound deductive argument whose premises include at least one general law and whose conclusion is a statement of the event to be explained.
label: fact

text: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X, argues that testimony can never establish a miracle as more probable than its violation of the laws of nature.
label: reference

text: Since a miracle by definition is a violation of a well-established law of nature, the evidence against such a violation is always stronger than any human testimony in its favor, so belief in miracles on testimony alone is unwarranted.
label: fact

text: John Dewey, Art as Experience (Minton, Balch, 1934), argues that aesthetic value consists in the consummatory quality of an experience rather than in intrinsic features of a privileged class of objects.
label: reference

text: What makes an experience aesthetic is its having a unified, consummatory quality in which means and ends are integrated, rather than the presence of some special class of fine-art objects.
label: fact

text: Immanuel Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790), Book II, analyzes the feeling of the sublime as a response to objects that exceed our capacity for sensible representation.
label: reference

text: The feeling of the sublime arises when the imagination is overwhelmed by something vast or powerful, and reason then recognizes its own supersensible vocation in the very failure of sensory grasp.
label: fact

text: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (J. Johnson, 1792), argues that women, as rational beings, are entitled to the same education and moral standing as men.
label: reference

text: Since women share with men the rational nature on which moral agency and civic participation depend, any system of education or law that systematically restricts women on the basis of sex alone is unjust.
label: fact

text: Kenneth Arrow, 'Social Choice and Individual Values' (Cowles Foundation Monograph 12, Wiley, 1951), proved that no social welfare function can simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain, non-dictatorship, Pareto efficiency, and independence of irrelevant alternatives when there are at least three alternatives.
label: reference

text: No voting rule over three or more alternatives can jointly satisfy unrestricted domain, non-dictatorship, the Pareto criterion, and independence of irrelevant alternatives.
label: fact

text: Fama and French, 'Common risk factors in the returns on stocks and bonds', Journal of Financial Economics 33 (1993) 3-56, introduced the three-factor model augmenting the market factor with size (SMB) and value (HML) factors.
label: reference

text: Cross-sectional variation in average stock returns is captured reasonably well by three common risk factors: the market excess return, a small-minus-big size factor, and a high-minus-low book-to-market factor.
label: fact

text: Reinhart and Rogoff, 'Growth in a Time of Debt', American Economic Review 100 (2010) 573-578, reported that median real GDP growth falls noticeably once gross public debt exceeds roughly 90 percent of GDP, a finding later revised after spreadsheet errors were identified by Herndon, Ash, and Pollin (Cambridge Journal of Economics 2014).
label: reference

text: Cross-country data show a negative correlation between very high public debt-to-GDP ratios and subsequent real growth, though the strength and threshold of this relationship remain contested.
label: fact

text: Card and Krueger, 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania', American Economic Review 84 (1994) 772-793, found no evidence that the 1992 New Jersey minimum wage increase reduced fast-food employment relative to Pennsylvania.
label: reference

text: A natural experiment comparing fast-food employment in New Jersey and Pennsylvania around a minimum wage increase found no meaningful employment reduction in the treated state.
label: fact

text: Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson, 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation', American Economic Review 91 (2001) 1369-1401, used settler mortality as an instrument to identify a large causal effect of institutions on long-run per-capita income.
label: reference

text: Differences in long-run income across former colonies are largely explained by differences in early extractive versus inclusive institutions, rather than by geography alone.
label: fact

text: Kahneman and Tversky, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk', Econometrica 47 (1979) 263-291, documented loss aversion and a value function concave in gains and convex in losses, contrary to expected utility.
label: reference

text: People evaluate risky prospects relative to a reference point and treat losses as roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains are pleasurable.
label: fact

text: Jacob Mincer, 'Schooling, Experience, and Earnings' (NBER, 1974), estimated log-earnings as a linear function of years of schooling and a quadratic in experience, the specification now known as the Mincer equation.
label: reference

text: Log hourly earnings are approximately linear in years of schooling and concave in potential labour market experience, with each additional year of schooling typically associated with about an eight to ten percent earnings premium.
label: fact

text: Robert Solow, 'A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth', Quarterly Journal of Economics 70 (1956) 65-94, introduced the neoclassical one-sector growth model with diminishing returns to capital and exogenous technical progress.
label: reference

text: In a one-sector neoclassical growth model with diminishing returns to capital, long-run growth in output per worker is driven by exogenous technological progress rather than by capital accumulation alone.
label: fact

text: Robert E. Lucas Jr., 'Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique', Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 1 (1976) 19-46, argued that reduced-form parameters estimated under one policy regime are generally not invariant to policy changes.
label: reference

text: Econometric models whose coefficients are not derived from agents' structural optimization problems will generally mislead policy evaluation because agents adjust expectations when policy changes.
label: fact

text: Black and Scholes, 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities', Journal of Political Economy 81 (1973) 637-654, derived the closed-form price of a European option under geometric Brownian motion and no arbitrage.
label: reference

text: Under geometric Brownian motion for the underlying asset and a constant risk-free rate, the no-arbitrage price of a European call option admits a closed-form solution involving the cumulative standard normal distribution.
label: fact

text: Modigliani and Miller, 'The Cost of Capital, Corporation Finance and the Theory of Investment', American Economic Review 48 (1958) 261-297, showed that in frictionless markets firm value is invariant to capital structure.
label: reference

text: In a world without taxes, bankruptcy costs, or information asymmetries, the total value of a firm is independent of how that firm is financed through debt or equity.
label: fact

text: John Nash, 'Equilibrium Points in N-Person Games', PNAS 36 (1950) 48-49, proved existence of mixed-strategy equilibria in every finite n-player non-cooperative game.
label: reference

text: Every finite non-cooperative game with a finite number of players and strategies admits at least one equilibrium in which no player can benefit by unilaterally deviating, possibly in mixed strategies.
label: fact

text: George Akerlof, 'The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism', Quarterly Journal of Economics 84 (1970) 488-500, showed that asymmetric information about quality can cause adverse selection and market unraveling.
label: reference

text: When sellers know product quality but buyers do not, adverse selection can drive high-quality goods out of the market even when mutually beneficial trades exist.
label: fact

text: Michael Spence, 'Job Market Signaling', Quarterly Journal of Economics 87 (1973) 355-374, formalized education as a signal of innate productivity in a labour market with asymmetric information.
label: reference

text: Costly education can serve as a signal of underlying worker productivity in labour markets with asymmetric information, even when schooling itself adds no human capital.
label: fact

text: Diamond and Dybvig, 'Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity', Journal of Political Economy 91 (1983) 401-419, modeled banks as providing maturity transformation with multiple equilibria, one of which is a self-fulfilling run.
label: reference

text: Demand-deposit banks that transform illiquid long-term assets into liquid liabilities are vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs, which deposit insurance can eliminate by ruling out the bad equilibrium.
label: fact

text: William Vickrey, 'Counterspeculation, Auctions, and Competitive Sealed Tenders', Journal of Finance 16 (1961) 8-37, showed that the sealed-bid second-price auction has truthful bidding as a dominant strategy.
label: reference

text: In a sealed-bid second-price auction with private values, bidding one's true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy.
label: fact

text: Gale and Shapley, 'College Admissions and the Stability of Marriage', American Mathematical Monthly 69 (1962) 9-15, introduced the deferred acceptance algorithm producing a stable matching in two-sided markets.
label: reference

text: The deferred acceptance algorithm always produces a stable matching in a two-sided market with strict preferences, and the outcome is optimal for the proposing side.
label: fact

text: James Heckman, 'Sample Selection Bias as a Specification Error', Econometrica 47 (1979) 153-161, proposed a two-step estimator correcting for non-random sample selection using the inverse Mills ratio.
label: reference

text: Ordinary least squares regression on a non-randomly selected sample produces biased estimates unless the selection process is modeled explicitly, for example by including a correction term constructed from a first-stage probit.
label: fact

text: Imbens and Angrist, 'Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects', Econometrica 62 (1994) 467-475, showed that an instrumental variable identifies the local average treatment effect for compliers under monotonicity.
label: reference

text: Under monotonicity, an instrumental variables estimator recovers the average treatment effect for those subjects whose treatment status is shifted by the instrument, rather than for the full population.
label: fact

text: Dickey and Fuller, 'Distribution of the Estimators for Autoregressive Time Series With a Unit Root', Journal of the American Statistical Association 74 (1979) 427-431, derived the non-standard limiting distribution of the t-statistic for the unit-root null.
label: reference

text: The t-statistic for testing a unit root in an autoregressive process does not follow a standard normal distribution under the null, so tabulated non-standard critical values must be used.
label: fact

text: Robert Engle, 'Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation', Econometrica 50 (1982) 987-1007, introduced the ARCH family of models for time-varying conditional variances.
label: reference

text: The conditional variance of many financial and macroeconomic time series is itself time-varying and can be modeled as a function of past squared innovations.
label: fact

text: Engle and Granger, 'Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing', Econometrica 55 (1987) 251-276, established the equivalence between cointegrated systems and error-correction representations.
label: reference

text: When two non-stationary time series share a common stochastic trend, their deviations from that trend are stationary and can be represented as an error-correction mechanism.
label: fact

text: Mortensen and Pissarides, 'Job Creation and Job Destruction in the Theory of Unemployment', Review of Economic Studies 61 (1994) 397-415, developed the canonical search-and-matching model of equilibrium unemployment.
label: reference

text: Equilibrium unemployment arises naturally from a search and matching friction in which vacancies and unemployed workers meet through a stochastic matching function.
label: fact

text: John B. Taylor, 'Discretion versus policy rules in practice', Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 39 (1993) 195-214, proposed a simple rule setting the federal funds rate as a function of inflation and the output gap.
label: reference

text: A simple monetary policy rule that moves the short-term nominal interest rate more than one-for-one with inflation and in the same direction as the output gap tracks historical Federal Reserve behaviour reasonably well.
label: fact

text: Milton Friedman, 'A Theory of the Consumption Function' (NBER, Princeton University Press, 1957), formulated the permanent income hypothesis, whereby consumption depends on expected long-run income rather than current income.
label: reference

text: Households smooth consumption against transitory income fluctuations, so consumption responds much more strongly to changes in perceived permanent income than to transitory shocks.
label: fact

text: Lucas and Prescott, 'Investment Under Uncertainty', Econometrica 39 (1971) 659-681, solved a dynamic rational-expectations equilibrium model of industry investment under stochastic demand.
label: reference

text: In a rational-expectations competitive equilibrium, firms' investment decisions are consistent with the equilibrium stochastic process they generate for prices.
label: fact

text: Piketty and Saez, 'Income Inequality in the United States, 1913-1998', Quarterly Journal of Economics 118 (2003) 1-39, reconstructed the long-run share of income accruing to the top one percent from US tax return data.
label: reference

text: The share of total US pre-tax income going to the top one percent of earners fell sharply from the 1930s through the 1970s and then rose again from the 1980s onwards, approaching pre-Depression levels.
label: fact

text: Chetty, Hendren, Kline, and Saez, 'Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States', Quarterly Journal of Economics 129 (2014) 1553-1623, used de-identified tax records covering tens of millions of children to map intergenerational mobility across US commuting zones.
label: reference

text: Intergenerational income mobility in the United States varies substantially across regions, with some metropolitan areas exhibiting mobility rates comparable to the most mobile European countries and others much lower.
label: fact

text: Banerjee, Duflo, Glennerster, and Kinnan, 'The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 7 (2015) 22-53, reported modest impacts of microcredit access in Hyderabad.
label: reference

text: Randomized evaluations of microcredit in low-income urban settings have generally found modest effects on business creation and no transformative effects on household consumption or welfare.
label: fact

text: Elinor Ostrom, 'Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action' (Cambridge University Press, 1990), documented eight design principles under which communities successfully self-govern common-pool resources.
label: reference

text: Common-pool resources such as fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems can be sustainably managed by user communities themselves when institutions satisfy design principles such as clear boundaries, graduated sanctions, and collective-choice arrangements.
label: fact

text: William Nordhaus, 'An Optimal Transition Path for Controlling Greenhouse Gases', Science 258 (1992) 1315-1319, introduced the DICE integrated assessment model coupling a Ramsey growth model with a climate module.
label: reference

text: An integrated assessment model that couples a neoclassical growth framework with a simple carbon-cycle and temperature module can be used to compute optimal paths of emissions abatement and a social cost of carbon.
label: fact

text: Martin Weitzman, 'On Modeling and Interpreting the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change', Review of Economics and Statistics 91 (2009) 1-19, argued that fat-tailed uncertainty about climate sensitivity can dominate standard cost-benefit analysis.
label: reference

text: Standard cost-benefit analysis of climate policy can give misleading results when the distribution of possible climate damages has a sufficiently fat right tail, because expected marginal utility losses can be unbounded.
label: fact

text: Paul Krugman, 'Increasing Returns, Monopolistic Competition, and International Trade', Journal of International Economics 9 (1979) 469-479, developed a model of intra-industry trade driven by love-of-variety and increasing returns.
label: reference

text: Trade between similar countries in similar products can be explained by consumer preferences for variety combined with firm-level increasing returns to scale, even in the absence of comparative advantage.
label: fact

text: Marc Melitz, 'The Impact of Trade on Intra-Industry Reallocations and Aggregate Industry Productivity', Econometrica 71 (2003) 1695-1725, introduced firm heterogeneity into trade theory, with only the most productive firms exporting.
label: reference

text: Trade liberalization reallocates market share toward the most productive firms within an industry, raising aggregate industry productivity through selection into exporting.
label: fact

text: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson, 'The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States', American Economic Review 103 (2013) 2121-2168, estimated the impact of rising Chinese import competition on US commuting zones.
label: reference

text: Rising import competition from China between 1990 and 2007 caused significant and persistent declines in manufacturing employment, wages, and labour force participation in the most exposed US local labour markets.
label: fact

text: Charles Tiebout, 'A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures', Journal of Political Economy 64 (1956) 416-424, argued that mobile households reveal their preferences for local public goods by sorting across jurisdictions.
label: reference

text: When households can freely move across jurisdictions offering different bundles of local public goods and taxes, their location choices can efficiently reveal preferences and support an efficient provision of those goods.
label: fact

text: Feldstein and Horioka, 'Domestic Saving and International Capital Flows', Economic Journal 90 (1980) 314-329, documented a high correlation between national saving and domestic investment rates among OECD economies.
label: reference

text: Despite apparent international capital mobility, national saving rates and domestic investment rates are strongly correlated across advanced economies.
label: fact

text: Bernanke, Gertler, and Gilchrist, 'The Financial Accelerator in a Quantitative Business Cycle Framework', in Handbook of Macroeconomics Vol. 1C (Elsevier, 1999) 1341-1393, embedded costly external finance in a DSGE model.
label: reference

text: Balance-sheet frictions that make external finance more costly than internal funds amplify and propagate shocks through the business cycle.
label: fact

text: Robert Shiller, 'Do Stock Prices Move Too Much to be Justified by Subsequent Changes in Dividends?', American Economic Review 71 (1981) 421-436, showed that stock price volatility far exceeds that implied by the present-value model with constant discount rates.
label: reference

text: Aggregate US stock prices have historically been far more volatile than the ex-post present value of dividends, challenging simple constant-discount-rate efficient markets models.
label: fact

text: Mehra and Prescott, 'The Equity Premium: A Puzzle', Journal of Monetary Economics 15 (1985) 145-161, showed that the historical US equity premium is far larger than a representative-agent consumption-CAPM with plausible risk aversion can justify.
label: reference

text: The historical excess return of equities over safe bonds in the US is much larger than can be rationalized by a representative-agent consumption-based asset pricing model with conventional levels of risk aversion.
label: fact

text: Klemperer, 'Markets with Consumer Switching Costs', Quarterly Journal of Economics 102 (1987) 375-394, analyzed how switching costs soften price competition and can raise equilibrium prices.
label: reference

text: When consumers face costs of switching between suppliers, firms effectively compete for future market share by pricing low initially and then exploiting locked-in customers, leading to higher average prices than under frictionless competition.
label: fact

text: Bresnahan and Reiss, 'Entry and Competition in Concentrated Markets', Journal of Political Economy 99 (1991) 977-1009, estimated how the market size required to support each additional firm grows less than proportionally, indicating rapid convergence to competitive conduct.
label: reference

text: In small local markets, the population required to support each additional entrant rises sharply from monopoly to duopoly but flattens quickly, suggesting that competitive conduct is approached with only a handful of firms.
label: fact

text: Roth, Sonmez, and Unver, 'Kidney Exchange', Quarterly Journal of Economics 119 (2004) 457-488, designed matching mechanisms for paired kidney donation that are strategy-proof and produce Pareto-efficient outcomes.
label: reference

text: Paired kidney exchange programs can be organized through strategy-proof mechanisms that increase the number of feasible transplants relative to direct donation alone.
label: fact

text: Grossman and Hart, 'The Costs and Benefits of Ownership: A Theory of Vertical and Lateral Integration', Journal of Political Economy 94 (1986) 691-719, introduced the property-rights theory of the firm based on residual control rights over assets.
label: reference

text: The boundaries of the firm are determined by who holds residual control rights over assets when contracts are incomplete, because ownership affects ex ante investment incentives.
label: fact

text: Gary Becker, 'Human Capital: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis, with Special Reference to Education' (NBER, Columbia University Press, 1964), formalized investment in schooling and training as analogous to investment in physical capital.
label: reference

text: Schooling, training, and health can be modeled as investments that raise an individual's productivity and lifetime earnings, with returns that can be compared to those on physical capital.
label: fact

text: Michael Grossman, 'On the Concept of Health Capital and the Demand for Health', Journal of Political Economy 80 (1972) 223-255, modeled health as a durable capital stock that depreciates with age and can be augmented by investment.
label: reference

text: Individuals can be viewed as choosing a path of investment in health as a durable stock that yields utility directly and indirectly by expanding time available for work and leisure.
label: fact

text: Finkelstein et al., 'The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment: Evidence from the First Year', Quarterly Journal of Economics 127 (2012) 1057-1106, used the 2008 Oregon Medicaid lottery to identify causal effects of insurance coverage.
label: reference

text: Randomized access to Medicaid in Oregon increased healthcare utilization, reduced financial strain, and improved self-reported health, without detectable short-run effects on objective measures such as blood pressure or cholesterol.
label: fact

text: Romer and Romer, 'A New Measure of Monetary Shocks: Derivation and Implications', NBER Working Paper 9866 (2003, later published in American Economic Review 94, 2004, 1055-1084), constructed narrative-based monetary shocks from FOMC records.
label: reference

text: Monetary policy shocks constructed from narrative records of Federal Open Market Committee intentions produce larger and more persistent estimated effects on output and prices than shocks identified from simple reduced-form VARs.
label: fact

text: The IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2019, Chapter 4 'The Rise of Corporate Market Power and Its Macroeconomic Effects', documented a broad-based rise in firm-level markups across advanced economies since 2000.
label: reference

text: Firm-level markups over marginal cost have risen broadly across advanced economies since around 2000, with the increase concentrated among already-high-markup firms.
label: fact

text: David Laibson, 'Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting', Quarterly Journal of Economics 112 (1997) 443-478, introduced quasi-hyperbolic discounting into intertemporal consumption choice and analyzed commitment devices.
label: reference

text: People tend to discount the near future more steeply than the distant future, creating time-inconsistent preferences that can generate demand for illiquid savings vehicles as commitment devices.
label: fact

text: Clement Greenberg, 'Avant-Garde and Kitsch', Partisan Review 6 (1939) 34-49, argued that the historical avant-garde arose as a defence of high culture against the industrial production of kitsch.
label: reference

text: The twentieth-century avant-garde can be read as a response to the rise of industrially produced mass culture, with modernist art attempting to preserve the autonomy of aesthetic experience.
label: fact

text: Roland Barthes, Mythologies (Seuil, 1957), analyzed everyday bourgeois culture — wrestling, steak and chips, the new Citroen — as a second-order semiological system that naturalizes ideology.
label: reference

text: Everyday cultural objects and spectacles can operate as myths in a semiotic sense, encoding ideological meanings that their users experience as natural and self-evident.
label: fact

text: Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (Princeton University Press, 1957), proposed a systematic theory of modes, symbols, myths, and genres, arguing that literary criticism could be a coherent conceptual discipline.
label: reference

text: Works of literature can be classified within a structured system of modes and archetypes, allowing criticism to function as a coherent theoretical discipline rather than a series of isolated judgements.
label: fact

text: Charles Rosen, The Classical Style: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven (Norton, 1971), argued that the late eighteenth-century classical style was defined by the dramatic articulation of tonal areas through sonata form.
label: reference

text: The late eighteenth-century classical style of Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven is characterized by the dramatic articulation of tonal regions, with sonata form organizing large-scale harmonic tension and resolution.
label: fact

text: David Bordwell, Narration in the Fiction Film (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985), developed a constructivist theory of narration, distinguishing classical, art-cinema, historical-materialist, and parametric modes.
label: reference

text: Narrative cinema can be analyzed as a set of distinct modes of narration — classical Hollywood, European art cinema, Soviet historical-materialist, and parametric — each with its own stylistic norms.
label: fact

text: Erich Auerbach, Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (Princeton University Press, 1953; German original 1946), traced the changing representation of reality from Homer and the Hebrew Bible to Woolf.
label: reference

text: The depiction of everyday reality in Western literature undergoes major shifts across history, from the external clarity of Homer to the fragmented interiority of twentieth-century modernist prose.
label: fact

text: Rosalind Krauss, 'Grids', October 9 (1979) 50-64, argued that the grid functions as both a spatial and a mythic emblem of modernist art's ambition to be simultaneously anti-natural and self-contained.
label: reference

text: The grid is a recurring formal device in modernist visual art because it enacts the ambition of autonomy from nature while insisting on flatness and self-reference.
label: fact

text: Erwin Panofsky, Studies in Iconology (Oxford University Press, 1939), distinguished pre-iconographic description, iconographic analysis, and iconological interpretation as three levels of meaning in visual art.
label: reference

text: The interpretation of a painting can be organized into three levels: identifying what is depicted, recognizing conventional themes, and uncovering the broader cultural meanings the image expresses.
label: fact

text: John Berger, Ways of Seeing (BBC / Penguin, 1972), argued that oil painting as a genre is structured to celebrate private property and that the female nude is typically constructed for a male spectator.
label: reference

text: Traditional European oil painting often frames its subjects in relation to ownership, and the female nude in particular is composed to address an implied male viewer rather than the depicted woman's own experience.
label: fact

text: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935; Zeitschrift fuer Sozialforschung V, 1936), argued that photographic and cinematic reproduction destroys the aura of the original artwork.
label: reference

text: The reproduction of artworks through photography and film erodes the unique presence, or aura, that a single original object holds within a specific tradition and location.
label: fact

text: Edward Said, Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978), argued that European scholarly and literary representations of the Middle East constituted a discourse that both enabled and legitimated imperial rule.
label: reference

text: European scholarly, literary, and artistic representations of the Middle East historically formed a coherent discourse that supported and justified colonial domination of those regions.
label: fact

text: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, 'Can the Subaltern Speak?', in Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, ed. Nelson and Grossberg (University of Illinois Press, 1988), argued that the gendered colonial subaltern cannot be recovered through dominant epistemic frames.
label: reference

text: Women situated at the intersection of colonial rule and patriarchal structures are often rendered inaudible within the dominant archives and theoretical frameworks that purport to represent them.
label: fact

text: Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish (French ed. Gallimard, 1975; English ed. Pantheon, 1977), traced the historical shift from sovereign spectacle of punishment to disciplinary techniques of the modern prison.
label: reference

text: Modern Western societies shifted from public corporal punishment to disciplinary regimes of surveillance, classification, and timetable that train bodies and minds across schools, factories, and prisons.
label: fact

text: Laura Mulvey, 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', Screen 16 (1975) 6-18, argued that classical Hollywood cinema structures vision through an active male gaze and passive female image.
label: reference

text: Classical Hollywood cinema has typically organized point of view so that the act of looking is coded as masculine and active while women appear as the passive object of that gaze.
label: fact

text: Andre Bazin, 'The Ontology of the Photographic Image' (1945), collected in What Is Cinema? vol. 1 (University of California Press, 1967), argued that photography's indexical link to reality underwrites cinema's realist vocation.
label: reference

text: Because a photographic image is causally imprinted by light from the object photographed, cinema carries a distinctive commitment to reproducing the contingency and depth of the physical world.
label: fact

text: Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (Russian original 1928; English trans. University of Texas Press, 1968), identified a fixed sequence of thirty-one narrative functions underlying the Russian wondertale.
label: reference

text: Russian wondertales can be analyzed as variations on a limited, ordered sequence of narrative functions such as departure, testing, and return, performed by a small set of character roles.
label: fact

text: Mikhail Bakhtin, 'Discourse in the Novel', in The Dialogic Imagination, ed. Holquist (University of Texas Press, 1981), argued that the novel is defined by heteroglossia and the dialogic interplay of social voices.
label: reference

text: The novel as a genre is distinguished by its capacity to stage the interaction of many social voices and styles within a single work, rather than imposing a single authoritative discourse.
label: fact

text: Fredric Jameson, 'Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism', New Left Review 146 (1984) 53-92, argued that postmodern culture is characterized by pastiche, depthlessness, and a weakening of historicity.
label: reference

text: Late twentieth-century culture increasingly relies on pastiche and stylistic quotation, often losing the sense of historical depth and critical distance associated with earlier modernism.
label: fact

text: Harold Rosenberg, 'The American Action Painters', ARTnews 51, no. 8 (1952) 22-23, 48-50, reframed Abstract Expressionist canvases as arenas in which the artist performs an existential act rather than producing pictures.
label: reference

text: Abstract Expressionist painters such as Pollock can be understood as treating the canvas less as a surface for pictorial representation and more as a stage for a recorded physical act of painting.
label: fact

text: Michael Fried, Absorption and Theatricality: Painting and Beholder in the Age of Diderot (University of California Press, 1980), argued that eighteenth-century French painting sought to deny the beholder's presence in order to re-establish pictorial absorption.
label: reference

text: Eighteenth-century French painting increasingly pursued the fiction of absorbed figures oblivious to the viewer, treating this denial of the beholder as a condition of serious pictorial art.
label: fact

text: Nikolaus Pevsner, Pioneers of the Modern Movement from William Morris to Walter Gropius (Faber, 1936), narrated a teleological history of modern architecture culminating in the Bauhaus.
label: reference

text: An influential narrative of modern architecture presents its emergence as a development running from the Arts and Crafts movement through engineering advances to the Bauhaus under Gropius.
label: fact

text: Robert Venturi, Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (Museum of Modern Art, 1966), argued against the reductive purity of orthodox modernism in favour of an architecture of 'both-and' rather than 'either-or'.
label: reference

text: A major strand of late twentieth-century architectural thought rejected the purism of orthodox modernism and advocated buildings that embrace ambiguity, historical reference, and contradiction.
label: fact

text: Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (Random House, 1961), argued that vibrant urban life depends on dense, mixed-use neighbourhoods with short blocks, aged buildings, and street-level eyes.
label: reference

text: Lively and safe urban neighbourhoods tend to feature a mix of uses, short blocks, a range of building ages, and enough density to keep eyes on the street throughout the day.
label: fact

text: Adolf Loos, 'Ornament und Verbrechen' (lecture 1910; published in Les Cahiers d'aujourd'hui, 1913), argued that the cultural evolution of civilized peoples is marked by the removal of ornament from everyday objects.
label: reference

text: A central early-modernist argument held that the progress of design in industrial societies would be reflected in the elimination of unnecessary decoration from everyday objects and buildings.
label: fact

text: Gunther Schuller, Early Jazz: Its Roots and Musical Development (Oxford University Press, 1968), analyzed the musical innovations of Louis Armstrong and his contemporaries through detailed transcription and formal analysis.
label: reference

text: Louis Armstrong's recordings of the late 1920s introduced rhythmic and melodic innovations that transformed jazz from a collective ensemble style into a soloist-led art form.
label: fact

text: Susan McClary, Feminine Endings: Music, Gender, and Sexuality (University of Minnesota Press, 1991), argued that Western tonal music encodes gendered narratives through cadential structures and thematic oppositions.
label: reference

text: Western tonal music since the seventeenth century often codes its thematic and cadential structures along gendered lines, associating stability with masculine and disruptive otherness with feminine themes.
label: fact

text: Richard Taruskin, Stravinsky and the Russian Traditions (University of California Press, 1996), situated Stravinsky's neoprimitivist works in The Rite of Spring within Russian folk and liturgical sources.
label: reference

text: Stravinsky's early ballets, including The Rite of Spring, draw extensively on Russian folk melodies and ritual traditions, rather than being a break with tradition in favour of pure modernism.
label: fact

text: Leonard B. Meyer, Emotion and Meaning in Music (University of Chicago Press, 1956), argued that musical affect arises from the confirmation and violation of learned stylistic expectations.
label: reference

text: Listeners experience musical emotion largely through the way a piece plays with their learned expectations, fulfilling or frustrating implications built up by stylistic conventions.
label: fact

text: Fred Lerdahl and Ray Jackendoff, A Generative Theory of Tonal Music (MIT Press, 1983), proposed a formal grammar of grouping, metre, time-span reduction, and prolongational reduction for tonal music.
label: reference

text: The hierarchical structure of Western tonal music can be modelled by rule systems that segment pieces into groups, impose metrical structure, and derive tree-shaped reductions of pitch content.
label: fact

text: Heinrich Schenker, Der freie Satz (Universal Edition, 1935), presented the Ursatz and concept of structural levels as the foundation of his theory of tonal music.
label: reference

text: Tonal compositions of the common-practice era can be heard as elaborations of a small number of underlying voice-leading structures that prolong tonic-dominant-tonic motion across an entire work.
label: fact

text: Sergei Eisenstein, 'A Dialectic Approach to Film Form' (1929), collected in Film Form, trans. Leyda (Harcourt, 1949), theorized montage as the collision of conflicting shots to generate new meaning dialectically.
label: reference

text: A classical Soviet theory of montage treats film editing as the dialectical collision of shots, whose juxtaposition generates meanings not present in either shot alone.
label: fact

text: Gilles Deleuze, Cinema 2: The Time-Image (French ed. Minuit, 1985; English trans. University of Minnesota Press, 1989), argued that postwar European cinema produces direct presentations of time rather than sensorimotor action.
label: reference

text: Postwar European art cinema developed forms in which time is presented directly through duration and memory, rather than indirectly through goal-oriented action.
label: fact

text: Pascale Casanova, The World Republic of Letters (French ed. Seuil, 1999; English trans. Harvard University Press, 2004), described a stratified international literary space with dominant and peripheral centres of consecration.
label: reference

text: The global circulation of literature operates through a hierarchical system in which a few metropolitan cities act as dominant centres of consecration, while most national literatures occupy peripheral positions.
label: fact

text: Franco Moretti, 'Conjectures on World Literature', New Left Review 1 (2000) 54-68, proposed 'distant reading' as a mode of literary analysis that treats systems rather than individual texts as primary objects.
label: reference

text: One response to the sheer scale of world literature is to replace close reading of individual canonical works with comparative study of large-scale patterns across genres, languages, and markets.
label: fact

text: Lawrence Venuti, The Translator's Invisibility: A History of Translation (Routledge, 1995), criticized Anglo-American norms of fluent, domesticating translation for rendering the translator invisible.
label: reference

text: The dominant English-language tradition of fluent, idiomatic translation tends to efface the translator's role and to assimilate foreign texts to target-language stylistic norms.
label: fact

text: Gideon Toury, Descriptive Translation Studies and Beyond (John Benjamins, 1995), argued that translations should be studied as facts of their target culture, governed by translational norms.
label: reference

text: Translations can be analyzed empirically as products shaped by the literary and social norms of the culture that receives them, rather than evaluated only against the source text.
label: fact

text: Stuart Hall, 'Encoding/Decoding' (1973; published in Culture, Media, Language, Hutchinson, 1980), argued that audiences may adopt dominant, negotiated, or oppositional readings of a televisual message.
label: reference

text: A single televisual message does not uniquely determine its reception; audiences can accept its preferred meaning, modify it, or read it against the grain depending on their social position.
label: fact

text: Raymond Williams, Marxism and Literature (Oxford University Press, 1977), developed the concept of 'structures of feeling' to capture emergent experiences not yet codified in dominant ideology.
label: reference

text: Cultures at any given moment contain emergent patterns of shared experience that have not yet hardened into explicit ideology, and literature often registers these structures of feeling first.
label: fact

text: Theodor W. Adorno and Max Horkheimer, 'The Culture Industry: Enlightenment as Mass Deception', in Dialectic of Enlightenment (Querido, 1947), argued that industrially produced culture standardizes taste and blocks critical reflection.
label: reference

text: Industrially produced mass entertainment tends to standardize cultural products and the responses they elicit, working against the autonomous, critical reception associated with older notions of art.
label: fact

text: John Dewey, Art as Experience (Minton, Balch & Co., 1934), argued that aesthetic experience is continuous with ordinary experience intensified and unified, not a separate metaphysical realm.
label: reference

text: Aesthetic experience is not sealed off from the rest of life but arises when ordinary perceptual and practical activity is intensified, unified, and felt as a coherent whole.
label: fact

text: Arthur C. Danto, 'The Artworld', Journal of Philosophy 61 (1964) 571-584, argued that something becomes an artwork only against a theoretical atmosphere and history of art — the artworld.
label: reference

text: Whether a given object counts as a work of art depends not on its perceptible properties alone but on its position within a historically situated network of theories, institutions, and practices.
label: fact

text: Heinrich Woelfflin, Principles of Art History (German ed. 1915; English trans. Dover, 1932), proposed five polar pairs — linear vs painterly, plane vs recession, closed vs open form, multiplicity vs unity, absolute vs relative clarity — to characterize the shift from Renaissance to Baroque.
label: reference

text: The stylistic shift from Renaissance to Baroque visual art can be described through a series of formal polarities contrasting linear clarity and stable composition with painterly fluidity and dynamic recession.
label: fact

text: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, Epistemology of the Closet (University of California Press, 1990), argued that much of modern Western thought is structured by a crisis of homo/heterosexual definition since the late nineteenth century.
label: reference

text: A wide range of modern Western categories — including those in literature, law, and psychology — have been shaped by the unstable opposition between homosexual and heterosexual definitions that crystallized in the late nineteenth century.
label: fact

text: W. J. T. Mitchell, 'The Pictorial Turn', Picture Theory (University of Chicago Press, 1994), argued that late twentieth-century thought had undergone a shift from the linguistic turn to a renewed interest in images and visuality.
label: reference

text: Late twentieth-century humanistic inquiry increasingly turned from language-centred models of meaning toward the study of images, visuality, and their role in structuring knowledge and power.
label: fact

text: Joseph Kerman, 'How We Got into Analysis, and How to Get Out', Critical Inquiry 7 (1980) 311-331, argued that Anglo-American musicology had over-invested in positivist analysis at the expense of critical and hermeneutic engagement.
label: reference

text: Late twentieth-century musicology was criticized for focusing too narrowly on formal and analytic description of scores at the expense of interpretive, historical, and critical engagement with music.
label: fact

text: Victor Papanek, Design for the Real World: Human Ecology and Social Change (Pantheon, 1971), argued that industrial design had become complicit in producing wasteful, socially harmful products and should be reoriented toward real human and ecological needs.
label: reference

text: A long-running strand of design thought holds that industrial design has often served consumer markets in wasteful and ecologically damaging ways and should be refocused on genuine human and environmental needs.
label: fact

text: Adrian Forty, Words and Buildings: A Vocabulary of Modern Architecture (Thames & Hudson, 2000), traced the historical transformation of key terms such as 'space', 'form', 'function', 'design', and 'structure' within modern architectural discourse.
label: reference

text: Core vocabulary of modern architecture such as 'space', 'form', and 'function' carries a layered history in which each term's meaning has shifted substantially since the nineteenth century.
label: fact

text: E. H. Gombrich, Art and Illusion (Bollingen / Princeton University Press, 1960), argued that pictorial representation develops through schemata and correction, with artists always mediating perception through inherited conventions.
label: reference

text: Pictorial representation is never a direct copy of nature but always proceeds through inherited schemata that artists modify, so every era's 'realism' is conditioned by conventions of depiction.
label: fact

text: George Steiner, After Babel: Aspects of Language and Translation (Oxford University Press, 1975), argued that understanding even within a single language is a form of translation, and that translation is a fourfold hermeneutic movement.
label: reference

text: Understanding any utterance involves an act of translation, and translation between languages can be analyzed as a hermeneutic process of trust, aggression, incorporation, and restitution.
label: fact

text: W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley, 'The Intentional Fallacy', Sewanee Review 54 (1946) 468-488, argued that the author's intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging the success of a literary work.
label: reference

text: One influential position in twentieth-century literary criticism holds that the meaning and value of a literary work should be assessed from the text itself rather than from claims about the author's private intentions.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 Working Group I Summary for Policymakers (2021), statement A.1.2, reports that global surface temperature increased by 1.09 degrees Celsius in 2011 to 2020 relative to 1850 to 1900.
label: reference

text: Global mean surface temperature in the 2011 to 2020 decade was about 1.1 degrees Celsius higher than the 1850 to 1900 pre-industrial baseline.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 WGI Summary for Policymakers (2021), statement A.1, concludes that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land.
label: reference

text: Human activities are the dominant cause of observed warming of the atmosphere, ocean, and land since the mid-twentieth century.
label: fact

text: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory data from the Mauna Loa Observatory reported a 2023 annual mean atmospheric CO2 mole fraction of 421.1 parts per million, the highest in the instrumental record.
label: reference

text: The annual mean atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration at Mauna Loa reached about 421 parts per million in 2023, the highest level ever directly measured.
label: fact

text: Luthi et al., Nature 453 (2008) 379-382, extended the EPICA Dome C ice core CO2 record to 800,000 years and showed atmospheric CO2 stayed between 172 and 300 parts per million across that interval.
label: reference

text: Ice core records show that atmospheric carbon dioxide remained between roughly 170 and 300 parts per million throughout the past 800,000 years, well below present levels.
label: fact

text: Cheng et al., Advances in Atmospheric Sciences 40 (2023) 963-974, reported that global ocean heat content in the upper 2000 metres reached a new record in 2022, with 2022 exceeding 2021 by 10.9 zettajoules.
label: reference

text: The heat content of the upper 2000 metres of the global ocean reached a new record high in 2022, continuing a multi-decadal warming trend.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 5 (2021) assesses that the surface open ocean pH has declined by approximately 0.017 to 0.027 units per decade since the late 1980s due to uptake of anthropogenic CO2.
label: reference

text: Uptake of human-emitted carbon dioxide has lowered surface ocean pH by roughly 0.02 units per decade since the 1980s, a process known as ocean acidification.
label: fact

text: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v3 records show the September Arctic sea ice extent has declined at about 12.6 percent per decade relative to the 1981 to 2010 mean.
label: reference

text: September Arctic sea ice extent has been shrinking at roughly 13 percent per decade relative to the late twentieth century average.
label: fact

text: The IMBIE Team, Nature 579 (2020) 233-239, estimated that the Greenland Ice Sheet lost 3902 plus-or-minus 342 gigatonnes of ice between 1992 and 2018, contributing 10.8 millimetres to global sea level.
label: reference

text: The Greenland Ice Sheet lost nearly 4000 gigatonnes of mass between 1992 and 2018, raising global mean sea level by about 11 millimetres.
label: fact

text: The IMBIE Team, Nature 558 (2018) 219-222, reported that the Antarctic Ice Sheet lost 2720 plus-or-minus 1390 gigatonnes between 1992 and 2017, with accelerating losses from West Antarctica.
label: reference

text: The Antarctic Ice Sheet has lost mass since 1992 with an accelerating trend driven primarily by ice shelf thinning and glacier retreat in West Antarctica.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 9 (2021) assesses that global mean sea level rose by 0.20 metres between 1901 and 2018 and that the rate accelerated to 3.7 millimetres per year during 2006 to 2018.
label: reference

text: Global mean sea level rose about 20 centimetres between 1901 and 2018, with the rate accelerating to nearly 4 millimetres per year after 2006.
label: fact

text: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement (UNFCCC, 2015) sets the long-term goal of holding the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5 degrees.
label: reference

text: Parties to the Paris Agreement committed to holding global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.
label: fact

text: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer (UNEP, 1987) mandated the phased elimination of chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting substances, with subsequent amendments including the 2016 Kigali Amendment on hydrofluorocarbons.
label: reference

text: An international treaty phased out chlorofluorocarbons and related ozone-depleting substances, later extended to cover hydrofluorocarbons, which are potent greenhouse gases.
label: fact

text: WMO Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022 projects that Antarctic springtime ozone will return to 1980 values around 2066 if current compliance with the Montreal Protocol continues.
label: reference

text: Antarctic springtime stratospheric ozone is projected to recover to its 1980 values around the mid-2060s if nations continue to comply with the existing ozone-protection treaty.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 5 Table 5.8 (2021) estimates the remaining carbon budget from the start of 2020 for a 50 percent chance of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees at 500 gigatonnes of CO2.
label: reference

text: The remaining budget of carbon dioxide emissions consistent with a 50 percent chance of staying under 1.5 degrees of warming was about 500 gigatonnes as of the start of 2020.
label: fact

text: Friedlingstein et al., 'Global Carbon Budget 2023', Earth System Science Data 15 (2023) 5301-5369, report that fossil CO2 emissions reached 36.8 gigatonnes in 2022 and constitute about 90 percent of total anthropogenic CO2 emissions.
label: reference

text: Fossil fuel combustion and industrial processes released about 37 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide in 2022 and account for roughly 90 percent of all human-caused CO2 emissions.
label: fact

text: Friedlingstein et al., 'Global Carbon Budget 2023', ESSD 15 (2023) 5301-5369, estimate that land and ocean sinks together absorbed about 54 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions over 2013 to 2022.
label: reference

text: Natural land and ocean sinks together remove roughly half of human-emitted carbon dioxide from the atmosphere each year, slowing the build-up of atmospheric CO2.
label: fact

text: Hansen et al., Science 342 (2013) 850-853, mapped global forest cover change at 30 metre resolution and estimated a gross loss of 2.3 million square kilometres of tree cover between 2000 and 2012.
label: reference

text: Roughly 2.3 million square kilometres of tree cover were lost worldwide between 2000 and 2012, with hotspots concentrated in the tropics.
label: fact

text: Gatti et al., Nature 595 (2021) 388-393, used aircraft observations to show that the southeastern Amazon has become a net source of atmospheric CO2, driven by deforestation and climate warming.
label: reference

text: Parts of the southeastern Amazon rainforest have switched from net carbon sink to net source in recent years, largely due to deforestation and warming.
label: fact

text: Hughes et al., Nature 543 (2017) 373-377, documented mass bleaching of the Great Barrier Reef in 2016, with 91 percent of surveyed reefs showing bleaching and strong correlation with degree-heating-weeks.
label: reference

text: A 2016 marine heatwave triggered widespread coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef, affecting more than 90 percent of the reefs that were surveyed.
label: fact

text: IPBES Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (2019) estimates that around one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades.
label: reference

text: Roughly one million animal and plant species are currently at risk of extinction, many within the coming decades, according to global biodiversity assessments.
label: fact

text: Hallmann et al., PLOS ONE 12 (2017) e0185809, reported a 76 percent decline in total flying insect biomass in German protected areas over 27 years of Malaise-trap sampling.
label: reference

text: Long-term monitoring in German nature reserves recorded a decline of roughly three-quarters in flying insect biomass over 27 years.
label: fact

text: Oliver et al., Nature Communications 9 (2018) 1324, analysed satellite records and reported that marine heatwave days increased by 54 percent globally between 1925 and 2016.
label: reference

text: The number of marine heatwave days worldwide has risen by more than half over the past century as the ocean surface has warmed.
label: fact

text: Kossin et al., PNAS 117 (2020) 11975-11980, found a global increase in the probability of major tropical cyclone intensity of about 8 percent per decade over 1979 to 2017 in satellite-derived data.
label: reference

text: The share of tropical cyclones reaching major hurricane intensity has increased by roughly 8 percent per decade since 1979.
label: fact

text: Philip et al., Earth System Dynamics 13 (2022) 1689-1713, attributed the 2022 western European heatwave to human-induced climate change, concluding such events are now about ten times more likely than in a pre-industrial climate.
label: reference

text: Heatwaves as severe as the 2022 western European event are now roughly ten times more likely than they would have been without human-caused climate change.
label: fact

text: IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 11 (2021) assesses that heavy precipitation events over most land areas have intensified at a rate broadly consistent with the Clausius-Clapeyron scaling of about 7 percent per degree of warming.
label: reference

text: Heavy precipitation events over most land areas have become more intense, with atmospheric water vapour capacity increasing by roughly 7 percent for each degree of warming.
label: fact

text: Williams et al., Nature Climate Change 12 (2022) 232-234, concluded that the 2000 to 2021 drought in southwestern North America was the driest 22-year period in at least 1200 years as reconstructed from tree rings.
label: reference

text: The 2000 to 2021 drought in southwestern North America was the driest 22-year span in the region in at least twelve centuries.
label: fact

text: Caesar et al., Nature Geoscience 14 (2021) 118-120, reconstructed the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation from proxies and reported that it is at its weakest in more than a millennium.
label: reference

text: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is now weaker than at any point in the past thousand years, based on multi-proxy reconstructions.
label: fact

text: Schuur et al., Nature 520 (2015) 171-179, estimated that northern permafrost soils contain about 1460 to 1600 petagrams of organic carbon, nearly twice the current atmospheric carbon pool.
label: reference

text: Northern permafrost soils store roughly 1500 petagrams of organic carbon, almost double the amount currently in the atmosphere.
label: fact

text: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory data show that globally averaged atmospheric methane increased by 18.0 parts per billion in 2021, the largest annual growth in the modern record beginning in 1983.
label: reference

text: Atmospheric methane grew by 18 parts per billion in 2021, the largest one-year increase observed since systematic global measurements began in 1983.
label: fact

text: Solomon et al., Science 327 (2010) 1219-1223, showed that a decline in stratospheric water vapour after 2000 slowed the rate of surface warming by about 25 percent relative to the preceding decade.
label: reference

text: A post-2000 decline in stratospheric water vapour temporarily reduced the rate of global surface warming compared with the 1990s.
label: fact

text: Bellouin et al., Reviews of Geophysics 58 (2020) e2019RG000660, assessed the effective radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions as minus 1.0 watts per square metre with a range from minus 1.7 to minus 0.3.
label: reference

text: Aerosol-cloud interactions exert a net cooling influence on Earth's energy balance of roughly one watt per square metre, partially offsetting greenhouse warming.
label: fact

text: The WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines 2021 lowered the annual mean PM2.5 guideline to 5 micrograms per cubic metre, citing cumulative evidence that ambient fine particle pollution causes millions of premature deaths annually.
label: reference

text: The World Health Organization sets the annual safe limit for fine particulate matter at 5 micrograms per cubic metre; exposure above this level causes millions of premature deaths worldwide each year.
label: fact

text: EPA Integrated Science Assessment for Ozone and Related Photochemical Oxidants (EPA/600/R-20/012, 2020) concludes that short-term ozone exposure causes respiratory morbidity and premature mortality.
label: reference

text: Short-term exposure to ground-level ozone increases respiratory illness and premature mortality, particularly in vulnerable populations.
label: fact

text: IRENA, 'Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2022' (2023), reports the global weighted-average levelised cost of electricity from utility-scale solar photovoltaics fell from USD 0.445 per kilowatt-hour in 2010 to USD 0.049 per kilowatt-hour in 2022.
label: reference

text: The global average cost of electricity from utility-scale solar photovoltaics dropped roughly ninefold between 2010 and 2022, falling below five US cents per kilowatt-hour.
label: fact

text: IRENA, 'Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2022' (2023), reports that the global weighted-average LCOE of onshore wind fell from USD 0.107 per kWh in 2010 to USD 0.033 per kWh in 2022.
label: reference

text: The global average cost of onshore wind electricity has fallen by nearly 70 percent since 2010 to around three US cents per kilowatt-hour.
label: fact

text: IEA, 'Global EV Outlook 2023', reports that electric car sales reached 10 million in 2022, raising their share of new car sales to 14 percent globally.
label: reference

text: Electric cars accounted for about 14 percent of new passenger car sales worldwide in 2022, with total annual sales reaching 10 million units.
label: fact

text: The Glasgow Climate Pact, adopted at UNFCCC COP26 in 2021, calls on parties to accelerate efforts toward the phase-down of unabated coal power and phase-out of inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies.
label: reference

text: Parties at the 2021 UN climate summit agreed to accelerate the phase-down of unabated coal power and phase out inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies.
label: fact

text: IEA, 'CCUS in Clean Energy Transitions' (2023), reports that around 45 commercial facilities capture about 45 million tonnes of CO2 per year globally, well below the scale envisaged in net-zero scenarios.
label: reference

text: Operating carbon-capture facilities worldwide remove around 45 million tonnes of CO2 per year, a small fraction of what net-zero scenarios require.
label: fact

text: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 'Reflecting Sunlight' (2021), recommends a cautious, federally coordinated research programme on solar geoengineering while emphasising that it is not a substitute for emissions reduction.
label: reference

text: Expert panels recommend cautious, government-coordinated research on solar geoengineering while stressing that it cannot substitute for cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
label: fact

text: Tilmes et al., JGR Atmospheres 123 (2018) 4616-4641, used CESM1 simulations to show that stratospheric aerosol injection could offset tropospheric warming but would alter regional precipitation and monsoon circulations.
label: reference
